The Case for Abolishing or Severely Restricting the Insanity Defense

The insanity defense is a relic of outdated 19th-century psychiatry and Victorian moral sentiment that has no place in a modern system of criminal justice grounded in personal responsibility, public safety, and equality before the law. It allows individuals who commit serious crimes—often violent ones—to escape conviction or receive dramatically reduced punishment on the theory that “mental illness” rendered them unable to control their actions or understand their wrongfulness. This doctrine is philosophically incoherent, empirically unreliable, prone to abuse, and fundamentally unjust. Mental illness should not function as a get-out-of-jail-free card. It is time to abolish the insanity defense outright or restrict it so narrowly that it becomes practically unavailable except in the most extreme and objectively verifiable cases.

Responsibility Is the Foundation of Criminal Law

Criminal punishment rests on two pillars: culpability (the defendant chose to do wrong) and deterrence (others must fear the consequences of similar choices). The insanity defense undermines both. It treats certain mentally disordered offenders as non-persons who lack agency, even when their actions demonstrate clear goal-directed behavior, planning, concealment, or motive. A person who hears voices commanding violence, yet methodically acquires a weapon, waits for an opportunity, and then attempts to evade capture, has displayed sufficient practical reasoning to be held accountable. The law already distinguishes between mere impulse and volitional incapacity in countless other contexts (addiction, provocation, duress). Singling out “mental illness” for special exemption is arbitrary.

Most severe mental disorders exist on a spectrum. Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and depression impair functioning to varying degrees, but forensic psychiatrists routinely admit on cross-examination that even floridly psychotic patients retain areas of intact cognition. The legal tests—whether the famous M’Naghten rule (“did not know the nature and quality of the act or that it was wrong”) or the more expansive American Law Institute test that includes “substantial capacity” to conform conduct to the law—are inherently subjective. They invite dueling expert witnesses who interpret the same clinical data to reach opposite legal conclusions. Juries are asked to decide metaphysical questions about free will that philosophers have debated for centuries. The result is not justice but a lottery.

Empirical Failure and the “Wrong” People Go Free

Data from jurisdictions that have retained broad insanity defenses show that the defense is invoked in only a tiny fraction of cases (roughly 1% or less), but when it succeeds the outcomes are troubling. Successful insanity acquittees are disproportionately charged with serious violent offenses—homicide, attempted homicide, and sexual assault—precisely the crimes that most alarm the public. In many systems, those found “not guilty by reason of insanity” (NGRI) spend less time in secure psychiatric facilities than comparable convicted defendants spend in prison. Release decisions are often made by mental-health professionals who prioritize treatment over punishment and risk assessment. The public correctly perceives this as a failure of justice: a person can commit a heinous act, be labeled “sick,” and eventually walk free while victims and society receive no moral accounting.

High-profile cases reinforce the perception of unfairness. When a defendant who meticulously plans an attack, writes manifestos, targets specific victims, and then claims voices or delusions, the spectacle of highly paid experts debating whether he “appreciated” the wrongfulness of his conduct undermines confidence in the courts. The defense also creates perverse incentives. Defense attorneys have strong reason to shop for sympathetic psychiatrists; prosecutors must expend enormous resources to rebut them. The entire process medicalizes what is, at bottom, a moral and legal judgment.

Mental Illness Explains but Does Not Excuse

No serious person denies that mental illness can be tragic, biologically real, and causally related to criminal behavior. Schizophrenia increases the statistical risk of violence; certain personality disorders correlate strongly with antisocial conduct; substance-induced psychoses can produce temporary breaks with reality. These facts should influence sentencing, conditions of confinement, treatment mandates, and civil commitment after punishment. They should not negate culpability entirely.

We do not excuse other powerful internal states. A person driven by overwhelming rage, jealousy, or greed is not permitted to claim “I could not help myself.” An addict who commits robbery to feed a habit receives limited mitigation at best. Poverty, childhood trauma, low IQ, and emotional abuse all powerfully predict crime, yet we rightly reject them as full defenses. To elevate psychiatric conditions above all other human frailties is to embrace a radical deterministic view that is inconsistent with how the law treats every other citizen. It implies that only the “normal” person possesses true free will—an assumption both arrogant and unprovable.

Moreover, many forms of mental illness are treatable. Modern psychopharmacology, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and structured programs can reduce symptoms and improve impulse control. The insanity defense, by framing the actor as fundamentally “not responsible,” discourages the very personal agency that treatment requires. It tells the defendant and society that the illness, not the person, committed the crime.

Practical Alternatives

Abolishing the insanity defense does not require cruelty or neglect. Several principled alternatives exist:

  1. Guilty but Mentally Ill (GBMI) verdicts, already used in some jurisdictions, allow conviction while mandating psychiatric treatment during incarceration. The sentence length remains tied to the crime, not the fluctuating opinion of hospital review boards.

  2. Diminished capacity or mitigation at sentencing. Evidence of mental disorder can reduce a specific-intent crime to a lesser offense or serve as powerful mitigation in capital cases and sentencing hearings, without creating an outright acquittal.

  3. Tightening the legal test. If any defense remains, it should be limited to the narrowest M’Naghten-style cognitive test supported by objective evidence—gross delusions that the victim was not human, for example, or frank delirium. Volitional prongs (“irresistible impulse”) should be eliminated entirely; they are impossible to falsify.

  4. Post-conviction civil commitment. Dangerous offenders who remain severely mentally ill after serving their sentence can be civilly committed under existing dangerousness standards (Kansas v. Hendricks, etc.). This separates the questions of past responsibility and future risk.

These reforms preserve the moral distinction between illness and wickedness while protecting the public. They also eliminate the spectacle of expert witnesses battling over whether a defendant “lacked substantial capacity” to conform his conduct to the law—an inquiry that too often becomes a proxy for jurors’ sympathy or disgust rather than a reliable assessment of blameworthiness.

Equality Before the Law

The insanity defense violates the principle that all competent adults are equal before the criminal law. It creates two classes of citizens: those whose psychological difficulties count as an excuse and those whose equally real sufferings (grief, trauma, personality flaws, addiction) do not. This is incompatible with liberal notions of personal dignity and accountability. If we truly believe individuals with mental illness possess moral worth, we must treat them as agents capable of responsibility rather than as perpetual wards of the state whose actions carry no moral weight.

Victims deserve to see their attackers held accountable under the same standards applied to everyone else. Society deserves a criminal justice system that communicates a clear normative message: certain acts are so wrong that no psychiatric explanation erases their wrongness. Treatment is a humanitarian concern, but it is not a substitute for justice.

The insanity defense is an anachronism that confuses compassion with weakness, psychiatry with jurisprudence, and explanation with excuse. It should be abolished or reduced to a vanishingly narrow exception. Mental illness may help us understand why a crime occurred; it should rarely, if ever, allow the perpetrator to escape the legal and moral consequences of what he deliberately chose to do. Responsibility, not therapy, must remain the default position of the criminal law.

The Debate Over the Insanity Defense

The insanity defense is a legal concept that allows defendants to be found "not guilty by reason of insanity" if they were unable to understand the nature of their actions or distinguish right from wrong at the time of the crime due to severe mental illness. The debate over its validity and application is multifaceted.

Arguments for Abolishing or Restricting the Defense

Proponents of abolishing or significantly restricting the insanity defense often argue from the perspectives of public safety, accountability, and legal simplicity.

  1. Accountability and Justice for Victims: Critics argue that the defense allows dangerous individuals to evade punishment, which can be deeply distressing for victims and their families. They contend that committing a violent act should result in consequences regardless of the perpetrator’s mental state.
  2. Potential for Abuse: Some believe the defense is susceptible to manipulation, where defendants might feign mental illness to avoid prison sentences. Although empirical studies suggest this is rare, the perception of it being a "loophole" persists.
  3. Difficulty in Determination: Assessing a defendant’s mental state at the time of a past crime is inherently challenging. Critics argue that psychiatric evaluations are subjective and can lead to inconsistent legal outcomes.
  4. Public Safety Concerns: There is concern that individuals found not guilty by reason of insanity may be released back into society sooner than they would have been if convicted, potentially posing a risk to public safety.

Arguments for Retaining the Defense

Supporters of the insanity defense emphasize principles of moral culpability, medical accuracy, and humane treatment.

  1. Moral Culpability: A foundational principle of criminal law is that punishment should be reserved for those who are morally blameworthy. If a person lacks the capacity to understand their actions due to severe mental illness, supporters argue they cannot be held morally responsible in the same way as a sane individual.
  2. Medical Reality: Mental illnesses such as schizophrenia or severe bipolar disorder can profoundly distort reality. Advocates argue that the legal system should recognize these medical realities rather than punishing individuals for symptoms of their illness.
  3. Treatment Over Punishment: The insanity defense often results in commitment to psychiatric facilities rather than prison. Supporters argue this is more appropriate and effective for individuals whose primary issue is mental health, aiming for treatment and rehabilitation rather than retribution.
  4. Legal Precedent and Fairness: The defense has deep roots in common law and is seen as a safeguard against unjust punishment. It ensures that the legal system accounts for extreme cases where intent (mens rea) cannot be established due to mental incapacity.

Current Legal Landscape

In the United States, the insanity defense is available in most jurisdictions but varies significantly in its application. Some states have abolished it entirely, while others use different standards, such as the M’Naghten Rule, the Irresistible Impulse Test, or the Model Penal Code standard. Federal law also has specific provisions under the Insanity Defense Reform Act of 1984, which narrowed the criteria for the defense.

The debate continues to evolve with advances in neuroscience and psychology, influencing how legal systems understand and address the intersection of mental health and criminal responsibility.
